sentences.text: Savannasaurus was a medium-sized sauropod dinosaur reaching approximately 15 meters in length.
This animal weighed around 20 tons and stood approximately 3 meters at the shoulder.
The creature is notable for its wide hips, which would have been over 1.1 meters wide at their widest points.
Its hips were exceptionally wide, measuring more than 1.1 meters across.
A theropod tooth found near the holotype suggests a predator may have fed on the specimen.
Savannasaurus is a sauropod dinosaur found in the Late Cretaceous Winton Formation of Queensland, Australia.
The first Savannasaurus specimen was discovered in March 2005 by David Elliot and his family.
The only known species, Savannasaurus elliottorum, was named in 2016 by Stephen Poropat and colleagues.
Savannasaurus was likely a sauropod with a wide-gauge posture, meaning it stood and walked with its feet very far apart from the midline.
The robust humerus of Savannasaurus is considered a likely adaptation to this wide-gauge stance.
In 2020, Poropat and colleagues pointed to the width of its sternal and sacral plates as evidence of a wide-gauge posture.
A flexible spine combined with wide hips and robust limbs likely helped Savannasaurus navigate the muddy floodplains where it lived.

Poropat and colleagues observed that both Savannasaurus and Diamantinasaurus likely lived in an alluvial plain with clay-rich soil and high rainfall, implying the ground would occasionally become muddy and dangerous for large sauropods.

Researchers considered it possible that environmental pressures selected individuals capable of navigating muddy terrain, and that Savannasaurus may have spent more time near water than other sauropods.
Flexible vertebrae to escape swamps, barrel-shaped bodies similar to hippos, a wide-gauge posture, and robust forelimbs to distribute body weight would have been useful for this niche.

While the environment might have selected for longer necks to access water, Poropat and colleagues observed that Savannasaurus and Diamantinasaurus likely had relatively short necks, though overlapping cervical ribs may have improved stability in Savannasaurus.

Savannasaurus possessed traits that increased vertebral column flexibility, specifically the absence of hyposphene-hypantrum articulations and prominent excavations below the transprezygapophyseal laminae.
Researchers suggested the unusual shape of the astragalus was an adaptation for weight-bearing, but the absence of other hind limb bones left this unclear.
Savannasaurus is classified as a basal member of the Titanosauria but not part of the specialized Lithostrotia group.
Mannion and colleagues found Savannasaurus within Saltasauridae in 2019 only when using equal weighting of characteristics, not implied weighting.
Savannasaurus lived during the Cenomanian to Lower Turonian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
Savannasaurus lived during the late Cretaceous, approximately 94 million years ago in the Turonian stage.
The rock unit containing Savannasaurus fossils, the upper Winton Formation, is dated to about 93.9 million years ago at the Cenomanian-Turonian boundary.
Palaeobiogeographic analysis suggests the ancestors of Savannasaurus were likely Asian.
Poropat and colleagues suggested that climate preferences might explain why Australian dinosaurs like Savannasaurus show affinities with Laurasian species.
It is debated whether the specific vertebral traits of Savannasaurus, such as the absence of hyposphene-hypantrum articulations, were unique adaptations or shared features with Diamantinasaurus.
Researchers postulated that saltasaurines may have been subject to similar selective pressures, so the typical titanosaurian body plan may have been acquired convergently several times.
